subject: dragonling
pitch: A baby dragon the size of a house cat, sitting proudly beside the broken shell of its speckled egg. Teal scales fading to a buttery belly, stubby horns, a row of soft orange spines down its back, oversized wings it can't fly with yet, with translucent amber skin between the fingers, and a chubby tail ending in a little spade. Big amber eyes, a toothy grin and a wisp of smoke curling from one nostril.
reasoning:
I'm sketching the overall scale and pose for the cat—sitting upright with haunches down and torso raised—and setting up a coordinate scheme where the dragon sits near the origin with the egg positioned slightly to its side.

Now I'm defining the skeleton hierarchy: a root hips joint, a spine chain running up to the chest, and a neck/head chain extending forward and up. I'm working out how to build the body mesh by sweeping a radius profile along the spine chain with a countershaded paint, and refining the chain point counts and names so the joint structure stays valid.

I'll just explicitly set spine2 as the parent to avoid ambiguity, then set up the neck sweep radius and build the head as the tip joint of a three-point neck chain, naming the joints neck1, neck2, and head.

For the head itself, I'm placing the cranium as a scaled sphere, adding a separate upper jaw frustum box for the snout, and giving the lower jaw its own joint and rod shape so it can hinge independently, plus small cone shapes along the upper jaw edge to suggest teeth.

Now I'm sketching out the actual dimensions — cranium radius, snout box tapering, jaw box proportions and joint position — then checking that against a realistic sitting cat height and deciding to scale the whole head down by about 25% to match proportions better.

Still placing head geometry...

Still placing teeth cones...

Now adding nostril details with tiny dark spheres and a wispy chain of translucent gray spheres curving upward to suggest smoke.

For the eyes, I'm placing amber spheres on the cranium surface with smaller black pupils offset outward and a white highlight sphere, considering a slit shape using a scaled sphere for the pupil.

For the horns, I'll use cone-shaped spikes projecting from a base point on the head with a defined direction, length, radius, and color.

For the spine, I'm planning a row of soft cones running along the dorsal surface of the body, neck, and tail using the sweep geometry to position them correctly.

Good, that confirms the back-facing direction logic works with flipping handled by the up-vector preference. Now I'm planning the spine scaling and colors along the neck and tail sweeps, then moving to the wings — oversized arm-bone chains starting from the shoulders at the back and extending up, outward, and back through elbow and wrist joints.

From each wrist I'm fanning out three finger chains with membranes stretched between them to form the wing surface, plus a membrane connecting the last finger back to the body. I'm structuring these as named point chains (shoulder, elbow, wrist, finger tips) so the membrane function can smoothly blend bone weights across the connected edges.

Also I should connect the arm chain to the first finger chain as the propatagium, the leading-edge membrane at the top of the wing, since the arm forms the front edge with fingers trailing behind. And I need a membrane from the last finger back to the body for the trailing edge.

I'll skip the arm-to-finger membrane and just add webbing between fingers and down to the body, keeping the wrist area simple. The wings should look oversized and not-quite-flight-ready, spread out T-pose style with bones rendered as tapering sweeps from thick arm radius down to thin fingertips.

For symmetry, I'll write one wing-building function parameterized by a sign flag so left and right mirror correctly, with naming suffixes L/R and consistent closed-prism membrane geometry that stays valid regardless of mirroring. I'm picking an amber translucent color for the membrane material.

Since true translucency isn't available, I'll fake it with a mottled paint gradient between lighter amber tones to give the membrane some visual depth. Now I'm planning the front arm chains—shoulder, elbow, wrist—so the dragon sits with hands resting on the ground in front of its chest.

Renaming to avoid collision with wing shoulders, I'm setting up the arm joints as upperArm, foreArm, and hand, parented to spine2, with tapering sweep radii. For the hand I'm flattening a sphere at the wrist for the paw shape, then adding three small claw spikes angled forward from the fingertips in ivory.

Now I'm adding toes as short capsule-based joints extending forward from the paw, spaced along x, each with a tiny claw tip, parented to handL with a "digit" role — keeping it modest rather than building full toe joint chains for all four limbs. Next I'm working out hind leg placement, sketching hip-to-knee positions for the sitting pose.

I notice the hind feet and front hands overlap in z-range, both near x=0.085 — I need to shift the arms inward to x=0.045 and move hand position to z=0.13, while pushing the hind feet outward to x=0.105 to avoid collision.

Working out precise joint coordinates for hip, knee, ankle, and paw on the hind leg, plus shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw on the front leg, checking that toe widths keep enough clearance between hand and foot positions, and confirming the thigh radius fits within the body radius without clipping. Now starting on the tail shape, aiming for a chubby profile.

Still defining tail chain...

Still shaping spade outline points...

Checking floor contact for the body: hips sink about 1.5cm, deeper than the 6mm tolerance, so I need to raise the spine's y-position and adjust its radius profile so the bottom cap rests right at the floor, then shift the neck position accordingly.

Now I'm propagating that offset through the head, nudging the cranium, eyes, snout, jaw, teeth, nostrils, and horns all upward by roughly a centimeter to stay consistent with the new body height, then checking that the shoulder and arm placement still align with the body's radius at that height.

Working out the paw, hand, thigh, knee, ankle, and foot proportions so the limbs taper correctly and the paw spheres sit flush against the ground, then starting on the wing shoulder and elbow joint positions.

Now I'm placing the wing arm joints and finger segments, extending them into a fanned, oversized span that reaches well above the head, which seems fine aesthetically even if it's a bit large.

I should set scallop depth around 0.08, and define membrane skin weighting between chain joints and bone references like "spine1". I'm also considering adding a membrane between the arm chain (shoulder to wrist) and the f1 leading edge, possibly skipping it for now and using a path instead.

Now I'm planning dorsal spines along the neck, back, and tail sweeps, using small cone geometries in a soft orange tone, scaling larger spines toward the back and reusing geometry where safe since meshes share it without cloning issues.

For the egg, I'm sketching a broken eggshell using a lathe profile with wall thickness and a jagged rim made of triangular teeth pieces, positioning it near the dragon's feet beneath the wing where it fits within the ground-level composition.

Verifying the polygon doesn't self-cross since the outer and inner edges stay separated by a thin gap. For coloring I'll use speckled paint with a cream base and brown spots, and for the jagged rim I'll add a ring of small wedge shapes at the top alternating heights to create broken shell shards.

Arranging shell wedge shapes...

I'll bind weighting explicitly to the egg bone rather than relying on nearest-joint inference. For the broken shell, I'm sketching a few curved shard pieces using partial sphere caps, positioning them lying on the ground with the dome side up so they look like fragments resting near the egg.

I'll skip adding crack lines or interior shell coloring since they won't be visible from above, and move on to defining the dragon's scale pattern -- a countershaded teal body with a lighter speckled back and a butter-toned belly.

Since the belly needs to face forward rather than downward while the dragon sits, I'm rethinking the countershading to use the normal's z-component instead of y, blending between back and belly colors with a smoothstep based on facing direction.

But I realize this same forward-facing rule breaks for the head, since the forehead also faces +z and shouldn't get belly coloring — so I need separate paint logic for the cranium versus jaw/snout, using y-based countershading there instead.

For limbs, tail, and arms I'll keep it simpler: mostly plain teal scales with countershading on the tail's underside, and I'm checking whether `paint.ts` exports the right helper functions like `resolve` and `mix` so I can blend two paints together inside a custom paint function.

I'm deciding which parts actually need the full painted gradient treatment versus plain color - body, neck, head, snout, jaw, limbs, tail, egg shell, and membranes get painted, keeping the resolution at 2048 for quality. The chubby belly look comes naturally from the body's sweep radius without needing separate shaping.

For the head details, I'm adding small spike-like ear frills jutting back from the sides rather than flat fin extrusions, skipping eyebrows and cheek blush, and letting the belly texture rely on scale painting rather than explicit stripe lines.

Now I'm checking the sweep and chain API details for the body: tuning radius arrays along the spine so hips, chest, and neck transition smoothly (like .07 to .08 to .062), verifying tail and rear sphere placement don't overlap awkwardly, and confirming the neck chain starts exactly where the spine path ends with matching radii.

I'm deciding to use catmull-rom interpolation for all the multi-point chains (body, neck, tail, limbs, fingers) so joints bend smoothly instead of sharply, since straight polylines would create hard kinks even with sweep fillets. I'm naming the joints along each chain (spine1/spine2, neck1/neck2/head) and setting parents correctly -- neck1 parents to spine2, arms also parent to spine2 -- while making sure the sweep calls reference these chains properly, with the head as a tip joint rather than a span.

Now I'm placing the jaw joint and sizing the lower jaw box to fit just under the snout, adjusting the y-centers and heights so the jaw overlaps slightly with the snout bottom without gaps, and positioning the teeth along the jaw's outer edge relative to the snout's width.

Widening the jaw from .05 to .034 lets the teeth peek out at the snout edges, giving it that grin look. I'll keep the lower jaw chin front flat-capped.

For the frustum shapes, I'm orienting the snout box along the Z axis with X as the creature's right and Y as up, keeping flat caps for the blocky style. Adding a snout block with its own paint color, then placing small spheres for nostrils near the tip.

I'm sweeping a smoke trail along a catmull-rom path rising from the nostril, tapering the radius with a simple function and giving it a soft gray color with rounded caps and low-poly sides.

Now I'm setting up a sphere helper for creating head geometry, then building the cranium as a slightly elongated sphere scaled along each axis and attached to the head bone, followed by small cheek puff spheres positioned on either side with a teal-pink tint.

Adding brow ridges and eye capsules...

Still calculating eye geometry...

Now I'm sketching the horns as stubby spike cones from the head base outward, keeping them simple with a tapered radius. I'm noting the arm joints will follow the earlier naming convention with shoulder, elbow, and hand points per side.

Setting up more joints...

Working out the hind leg ankle, paw, and toe positions similarly, then checking for overlap between the hand and hind paws on the x-axis — I'm nudging the hand position inward to avoid collision and adjusting the hand toe spread accordingly.

Now I'm setting up the wing structure: defining a teal-colored arm chain with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints parented to the spine, plus finger chains attached to the wrist for the wing digits.

Still adding wing details...

I'm setting up the amber mottled wing paint, adding a function to place dorsal spines along the body with sizes scaled by index, and defining the cone geometry for them.

Thinking through spine orientation — since sticks align along the outward normal, and the body tube's tangent is mostly vertical, I need to figure out the correct "up/back" normal direction so the spines actually run along the dragon's back rather than pointing sideways. I'm computing the flattened up-vector perpendicular to the tube's tangent to get the right placement direction.

Now I'm defining the color palettes — teal and butter scale paint functions with their own seeds, sizes, and widths — plus a belly paint function that blends in countershading based on the surface normal, which I'll need for the body and neck regions near where the arms attach.

For the egg texture, I'm blending the two color layers directly without branching for performance, then designing the speckle pattern — layering a mottled base coat with finer dark spots on top for a more natural egg appearance.

I'm setting up the lathe geometry for the egg shape, using 10 segments for a slightly low-poly look while keeping the profile orientation correct, then adding a jagged rim ring of teeth around the egg's inner opening using cone-shaped parts arranged radially.

I'll reuse the egg paint texture for consistency and add a simple pale yolk puddle inside the broken shell's bottom, keeping it minimal rather than adding extra nest or ground details since those weren't requested. Now I'm placing the egg at coordinates near the dragon's right hand.

Checking against the dragon's hind foot and toe positions, I need to nudge the egg further out to ex=-0.21, ez=0.13 so it doesn't overlap the foot. I'll keep the dragon's posture proud with chin up and chest out, confirm the wings and shards stay clear of the egg, then move on to finalizing colors and exporting.

Picking a dark orange for the tail spade, I'm now working out the extrusion parameters and positioning it at the tail's final point, aligning its center and radius with the tapering tail end.

Checking that the spade's curve direction clears the dragon's hind foot, I confirm the geometry avoids collision since the foot sits at a higher z-value. I'm setting up the tail chain's parent hierarchy under "hips," defining five path points and matching radii that taper from thick near the body to thin at the tip.

Now I'm moving to the belly paint on the body mesh, confirming it relies on the mesh's own normals so the coloring follows the surface correctly. I'm starting to write the actual sweep code for the body part, then defining a wing function that builds a chain for the wing arm using catmull-rom interpolation between shoulder, elbow, and wrist points, parented to the spine.

Writing wing sweep code...

Now I'm working out the finger chains that branch off the wrist joint, defining three roughly collinear point sets for varying finger lengths, and confirming the membrane geometry and mirrored wing orientation don't need special handling since default normals work fine.

I'm wrapping up the builder call and planning the nostril details and teeth placement, computing the snout's half-width and bottom edge as functions of z-position so each tooth cone sits correctly along the jawline.

For the jaw joint, I'll make sure it carries a "jaw" role in its options, and decide to keep the mouth closed with teeth visible rather than posing it open for a grin.

Now I'm adding the egg's inner goo as a small cylinder part attached to the egg bone. For the eggshell shards, I'm writing a helper function that generates partial sphere caps with a given radius and rim angle, calculating the vertical offset so each shard's rim sits flush with the ground while the dome rises slightly above it.

Checking that no geometry dips below the floor, I keep the shards flat-shaded with elliptical scaling and y-axis rotation for variation, then proceed to write out the shard code.
